drills.q: Walk a packet from the wire to your application's recv() call.
drills.a: NIC DMAs the frame into an RX ring buffer and raises a hardIRQ; the handler does minimal work and schedules a softIRQ; NAPI's poll routine drains the ring in batches (default budget 64) instead of interrupting per-packet; the driver builds an skb, passed up via netif_receive_skb() -> ip_rcv() -> tcp_v4_rcv() into the socket receive queue, waking a blocked recv()/epoll_wait().

drills.q: What does interrupt coalescing trade off, and when would you tune it differently?
drills.a: ethtool -c settings (rx-usecs/rx-frames) batch more packets per interrupt, cutting CPU overhead under sustained load at the cost of added per-packet latency/jitter. Throughput-oriented bulk transfer benefits from aggressive coalescing; latency-sensitive workloads want it tuned down.

drills.q: What actually changed between TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3's handshake, in round trips?
drills.a: TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTT before app data. TLS 1.3 sends the client's key share speculatively in the first flight, cutting the full handshake to 1 RTT, plus an optional 0-RTT resumption mode with a replay-protection gap on that first flight.

drills.q: Explain TCP head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 precisely -- what guarantee causes it?
drills.a: TCP guarantees strictly ordered delivery for the entire connection as one byte stream with no concept of independent streams. A lost packet for stream A blocks delivery of all later-arrived bytes, including unrelated stream B's, until retransmission restores connection-wide order.

drills.q: How does QUIC solve TCP head-of-line blocking, mechanically?
drills.a: QUIC implements its own reliability/loss-recovery in userspace over UDP with independent per-stream sequencing. A lost packet on stream A is retransmitted independently; stream B's already-arrived data is delivered immediately, with no connection-wide ordering guarantee to violate.

drills.q: Why do browsers open 6-8 parallel connections per origin under HTTP/1.1, and what did that cost?
drills.a: HTTP/1.1 allows one request in flight per connection in practice; browsers parallelize connections to get real concurrency. Cost: each connection pays its own TCP+TLS handshake, multiplying fixed cost 6-8x, and distorts TCP's per-connection congestion-control fairness.

drills.q: A service's p99 has a consistent extra 150ms not showing in application tracing. What do you check, in order?
drills.a: Use curl -w per-phase timing (DNS, TCP connect, TLS handshake, TTFB) to attribute the 150ms to a layer. DNS -> check resolver cache/TTL. TCP/TLS connect -> check connection reuse/pooling. Fast connect but slow TTFB -> the problem is in the application/backend, not this stack.

drills.q: What is GRO and why does it matter for CPU efficiency?
drills.a: Generic Receive Offload coalesces multiple physically-received TCP segments of the same stream into one larger skb before upper-layer processing, reducing how often the more expensive IP/TCP processing runs per byte -- an amortization technique similar in spirit to NAPI's batched interrupt handling.

drills.q: Design: a mobile backend has clients frequently switching WiFi to cellular mid-session. What protocol choice addresses this, and why can't TCP do it?
drills.a: HTTP/3/QUIC. TCP identifies a connection by the 4-tuple (src/dst IP:port), which breaks entirely on an IP change, forcing full reconnect. QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID independent of IP, surviving the handoff with live connection state intact -- a property TCP can't retrofit without redefining what a connection is.

drills.q: What's the mechanical difference between HPACK header compression and just gzipping headers?
drills.a: HPACK keeps a stateful shared dynamic table across the connection's lifetime so repeated headers are referenced by a short index rather than resent, exploiting cross-request redundancy. Stateless per-message gzip can't do that, and compressing headers with attacker-influenceable and secret data together enabled CRIME/BREACH-style side-channel attacks, which HPACK's design deliberately avoids.

drills.q: Your team is deciding whether to migrate an internal, same-datacenter microservice mesh from HTTP/2 to HTTP/3. Make the case for and against.
drills.a: For: eliminates TCP-level HOL blocking, and connection migration helps if traffic crosses IP-changing boundaries (rare internally). Against: low-loss, low-latency internal traffic barely triggers the HOL-blocking problem QUIC solves, while QUIC's userspace implementation costs more CPU per byte than TCP's kernel-optimized path -- for a low-loss internal mesh this often favors staying on HTTP/2; reserve HTTP/3 for the internet-facing edge with real loss and mobile variability.
